entry.title: Why the Hidden Job Market Matters
entry.summary: If your job search consists mainly of watching job boards, applying for…
entry.content:
If your job search consists mainly of watching job boards, applying for advertised roles and waiting for recruiters to respond, you are seeing only part of the market.

Some opportunities are advertised.

Many begin much earlier.

They start with a conversation. A business problem. A recommendation. A recruiter testing the market. A leader asking someone they trust, “Who do you know?”

That is the hidden job market.

It isn’t a secret market and it isn’t a collection of jobs being deliberately kept from candidates. It is simply the part of the employment market where opportunities begin through relationships, reputation and conversations before — and sometimes instead of — becoming formal vacancies.

For experienced professionals, understanding this matters.

Senior opportunities often start before there is a job ad

The more senior the role, the less likely the process is to begin with an organisation simply posting a detailed advertisement and waiting to see who applies.

A business may know it needs different capability but not yet have defined the role.

A senior leader may be considering a restructure.

An executive search consultant may be mapping potential candidates before receiving a formal assignment.

A board member, investor, adviser or former colleague may know someone who would be a strong fit for a problem the organisation is trying to solve.

These situations create opportunities before there is anything to apply for.

By the time a role reaches a job board, conversations may already have taken place and potential candidates may already be known.

That doesn’t mean advertised roles are unimportant. They are one route into the market.

They just shouldn’t be the only one.

Applying and positioning are different activities

Traditional job-search advice tends to focus heavily on applications:

Find a vacancy.
Tailor your résumé.
Submit an application.
Wait.

There is nothing inherently wrong with that process. The problem comes when it becomes the entire strategy.

Experienced professionals usually have something more powerful available to them: years of relationships, expertise, reputation, industry knowledge and accumulated credibility.

The question becomes less:

“How do I apply for more jobs?”

and more:

“How do I become known, relevant and visible to the people who may influence my next opportunity?”

That is a positioning question.

Strong positioning means people can understand what you bring, the kinds of problems you are equipped to solve and where your experience is most relevant.

Without that clarity, even a strong network can struggle to help you.

Relationships matter — but this isn’t about networking for the sake of it

The phrase “hidden job market” sometimes leads people to think they need to network aggressively.

I don’t believe that is the answer.

Most experienced professionals dislike transactional networking for good reason. Contacting people simply because you want something rarely creates strong professional relationships.

A better approach is to have purposeful conversations.

Reconnect with people whose judgement you value.

Talk with people who understand the markets, organisations or sectors you are exploring.

Ask intelligent questions.

Share what you are thinking about.

Be interested in what is happening in their world.

The purpose isn't to ask everyone you know for a job.

It is to become part of the conversations in which information, introductions and opportunities naturally emerge.

That is a very different kind of networking.

Visibility matters more than many experienced professionals realise

One of the challenges of a long career is that we can assume our experience speaks for itself.

Often it doesn’t.

People know us through the context in which they last worked with us. Someone who knew you five or ten years ago may have very little understanding of what you can contribute today.

Others may respect you professionally but have no idea that you are considering a move.

This is why purposeful visibility matters.

It doesn't require becoming a constant social-media broadcaster or building an artificial “personal brand”.

It means making it easier for relevant people to understand:

  • what you do well
  • where your experience creates value
  • what you are interested in
  • and the kinds of conversations you are open to.

Done well, visibility helps your reputation travel further than your immediate network.

The hidden market is not a shortcut

There is an important distinction here.

Accessing the hidden job market is not about finding a clever way around normal recruitment processes.

It still requires clarity, credibility and effort.

Sometimes a hidden-market conversation leads directly to an opportunity.

More often, it leads to information.

Then another conversation.

Then an introduction.

Then greater clarity about where the market sees value in your experience.

Over time, those conversations create momentum.

That is why I tend to think of the hidden job market less as a place you “find” and more as a market you learn how to participate in.

A different way to think about career transition

For experienced professionals, career transition is rarely solved simply by submitting more applications.

A more useful approach is usually to work on three things:

Clarify your direction.
Understand the work you want to pursue and where your experience is most relevant.

Strengthen your positioning.
Make it easy for other people to understand the value you bring.

Access the hidden market.
Build the relationships, visibility and conversations that put you closer to opportunities as they emerge.

Job applications may still be part of the picture.

They are simply no longer the whole picture.

And that shift — from waiting for opportunities to be advertised to becoming better positioned for the conversations that create them — can fundamentally change the way you approach your next career move.

If you want to see how well positioned you currently are for the hidden job market, the Hidden Job Market Diagnostic provides a quick snapshot of where your approach is creating traction and where there may be gaps.

entry.title: Experience Is an Asset, Not a Liability
entry.summary: One of the more damaging assumptions experienced professionals can make during a…
entry.content:
One of the more damaging assumptions experienced professionals can make during a career transition is that their age or length of experience has somehow become a problem.

Sometimes the market does make experienced candidates work harder to demonstrate relevance.

But that is very different from saying experience itself is a liability.

Used well, experience is one of your strongest assets.

The challenge is not simply having it.

The challenge is positioning it so that other people can see its value.

Experience only helps if the market understands it

A long career creates depth.

You have seen more situations.

Solved more problems.

Worked with different personalities, markets, cultures, cycles and organisational realities.

You have probably learned things that are difficult to teach quickly.

But none of that automatically translates into value in the eyes of a prospective employer, recruiter or contact.

The market does not reward experience simply because it exists.

It rewards experience that appears relevant to the problem in front of it.

That is why experienced professionals need to move beyond simply describing what they have done.

The stronger question is:

What does all of this experience now enable me to do better, faster or with more judgement than someone with less of it?

That is where experience begins to become leverage.

The risk is sounding historical

Many experienced professionals unintentionally present themselves as a chronology.

They describe their career in order.

They list responsibilities.

They explain previous titles.

They provide context for roles that may have been important at the time but are not especially relevant to what comes next.

The result can be accurate but not compelling.

A senior professional should not need to prove they have had a career.

That is already obvious.

What matters is helping people understand the themes that run through that career.

What problems have you repeatedly solved?

Where have people trusted your judgement?

What kind of situations bring out your best work?

What has become easier for you because you have done it many times before?

These are much more useful signals than simply saying you have 20 or 30 years of experience.

Relevance matters more than recency

Another trap is assuming that only the most recent role counts.

Sometimes it does.

But often the most valuable part of someone’s background comes from earlier experience that has become highly relevant again.

A person may have built teams in a difficult market ten years ago and now find themselves speaking with an organisation facing exactly that problem.

Someone may have worked through a major restructure earlier in their career and now understand how to navigate change in a way others do not.

Another may have spent years building relationships across a sector and now have access, credibility and context that would take someone else a decade to develop.

The point is not to drag everything from your past into the present.

It is to identify which parts of your experience still have strategic value.

Senior careers are judged on judgement

As careers progress, technical capability still matters.

But increasingly, people are valued for judgement.

Can you read a situation quickly?

Can you distinguish between noise and what really matters?

Can you make sound decisions when the information is incomplete?

Can you influence people without needing formal authority?

Can you see patterns others miss?

Can you avoid mistakes because you have seen similar situations before?

These are not abstract qualities.

They are often the result of accumulated experience.

And in senior roles, that judgement can be far more valuable than simply being the person who has the newest technical skill.

Your experience needs a point of view

The strongest experienced professionals are usually not just repositories of knowledge.

They have developed a point of view.

They understand what good looks like.

They know what tends to work and what tends not to.

They can explain where organisations make mistakes.

They can recognise patterns.

That point of view helps other people understand why your experience matters.

It also creates visibility.

When you are able to speak clearly about your field, your market or the problems you solve, people begin to associate you with those issues.

That is useful in the hidden job market because opportunities often emerge when someone thinks:

“We should talk to them.”

Experience should create confidence, not complacency

There is an important distinction here.

Experience is valuable.

But experience alone is not enough.

The market changes.

Technology changes.

Expectations change.

The language organisations use changes.

Experienced professionals still need to stay current, curious and open to learning.

The objective is not to defend the past.

It is to combine what you already know with what the market now needs.

That combination is powerful.

Reposition the story

If you are an experienced professional in transition, it may be useful to stop asking:

“Will my age count against me?”

and start asking:

“How clearly am I showing the value of what I have learned?”

Your experience should not be presented as weight you carry.

It should be presented as capability you can deploy.

That means being selective.

Relevant.

Clear.

And able to explain how the accumulated judgement, credibility, relationships and perspective from your career can help solve the problems that matter now.

Experience is not automatically an advantage.

But when it is positioned well, it can be one of the strongest forms of career leverage you have.

entry.title: Networking Without Feeling Transactional
entry.summary: For many experienced professionals, the word networking creates an immediate sense of…
entry.content:
For many experienced professionals, the word networking creates an immediate sense of discomfort.

It can sound forced.

Self-promotional.

Transactional.

Like turning every conversation into an attempt to extract something from someone else.

That is not how I think useful professional relationships work.

Good networking is not about collecting contacts or asking people for favours.

It is about staying connected, being curious, exchanging useful information and building enough trust that conversations can lead somewhere over time.

Why networking often feels uncomfortable

The discomfort usually comes from the way networking is framed.

People are often told to:

  • reach out to as many people as possible

  • tell everyone they are looking for work

  • ask for introductions

  • request coffee meetings

  • “work the room”

  • follow up relentlessly.

For some people that approach may work.

For many experienced professionals, it feels unnatural.

And when it feels unnatural, the conversation often becomes awkward for both sides.

The problem is not relationships.

The problem is approaching relationships only when you need something.

Start with curiosity, not an ask

A better conversation often begins with genuine curiosity.

You may want to understand:

  • what is changing in a sector

  • how a particular organisation is thinking about an issue

  • where demand is increasing

  • what skills are becoming more important

  • how someone else is seeing the market

  • what challenges leaders are dealing with.

That creates a very different dynamic.

Instead of saying:

“Can you help me find a job?”

you are saying:

“I value your perspective and would like to understand what you are seeing.”

That is a more natural conversation.

It also tends to produce better information.

Relationships are not a short-term tactic

One of the biggest mistakes people make in career transition is treating networking as a project that starts when they lose a job and stops when they find one.

Professional relationships are more useful when they are part of normal working life.

That does not mean constant activity.

It simply means staying in touch with people you respect.

Checking in occasionally.

Sharing something useful.

Congratulating someone on a move.

Making an introduction when it helps.

Having a conversation because you are interested, not because you need an outcome.

Over time, that creates trust.

And trust is what makes relationships useful when important conversations arise.

You do not need a huge network

There is also a tendency to think that networking success depends on having thousands of connections.

It usually does not.

A smaller group of relevant, trusted relationships can be far more valuable than a large list of weak contacts.

Think about the people who:

  • understand your work

  • know your reputation

  • have seen you perform

  • operate in markets you care about

  • are connected to organisations or people relevant to your direction

  • are willing to have an honest conversation with you.

Those relationships often matter more than raw network size.

Be clear about what you are exploring

Networking becomes difficult when you cannot explain what you are interested in.

If your message is:

“I’m open to anything.”

people have very little to work with.

They cannot easily think of relevant organisations, people or opportunities.

You do not need to have every detail solved.

But you should be able to communicate enough direction for someone else to understand the kind of work, problems, sectors or environments you are exploring.

Clarity makes conversations easier.

It also makes introductions more useful.

Ask better questions

The quality of a networking conversation is often determined by the quality of the questions.

Instead of asking:

“Do you know of any jobs?”

you might ask:

  • What are you seeing in the market at the moment?

  • Where do you think organisations are struggling?

  • Which capabilities seem to be becoming more important?

  • Who else do you think would have an interesting perspective on this?

  • If you were in my position, what would you be paying attention to?

These questions invite insight rather than obligation.

And sometimes the most useful outcome of a conversation is not an opportunity.

It is a piece of information that changes your direction.

Give something back

Professional relationships work best when they are reciprocal.

That does not mean keeping score.

It means thinking about how you can also be useful.

You may have:

  • information

  • experience

  • introductions

  • perspective

  • encouragement

  • industry knowledge

  • a useful article or resource.

Often the best way to strengthen a relationship is simply to be someone worth staying connected to.

Do not force the next step

Not every conversation needs to lead somewhere immediately.

Some will.

Many will not.

That is normal.

The goal is not to turn every interaction into an opportunity.

It is to stay part of the professional conversation.

Over time, people remember people who are thoughtful, credible, useful and easy to engage with.

That matters because many opportunities begin with a simple thought:

“I know someone who might be worth speaking to.”

A more useful definition of networking

If the word networking still feels uncomfortable, redefine it.

Think of it as:

maintaining professional relationships and having useful conversations.

That is really what it is.

No performance.

No pretending.

No forced self-promotion.

Just staying connected to people, being interested in what is happening around you, and making it easier for useful conversations to occur.

That kind of networking does not have to feel transactional.

Done well, it feels like what strong professional relationships have always been.
